status: DRAFT, UNVALIDATED: items written for the Review 2 framework. They have not been reviewed by the instructor, piloted, or checked for difficulty or parallel-form equivalence. No student has taken them.
design: Two parallel forms: each learning objective has one pre-test item and one post-test item testing the same concept with a different surface. Scoring: mcq 0/1; short_answer and code_reasoning 0/1/2 by the rubric, normalised to [0, 1] per item.

fields.difficulty: easy | medium | hard (author's estimate, not calibrated)
fields.expected_concept: the concept a correct answer demonstrates
fields.answer: mcq: correct option letter; otherwise rubric points
fields.grounding_chunks: corpus chunk ids that teach the concept (from benchmark v1.1 grade-2 judgments)

items.expected_concept: threads share the address space but each has its own stack
items.question: Two threads of the same process both declare a local variable x inside their start function. Which statement is true?

options.A: Both threads read and write the same x
options.B: Each thread has its own x on its own stack
options.C: The second thread cannot be created until the first returns
options.D: x is stored in the heap and shared

items.expected_concept: threads share the address space but each has its own stack
items.question: Which of these is NOT shared between threads of the same process?

items.expected_concept: passing &i to pthread_create shares one variable that the loop keeps changing
items.question: for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) pthread_create(&t[i], NULL, worker, &i);  Each worker prints *(int *)arg. Why can the output show repeated or wrong numbers, and how do you fix it?
answer: All threads receive the address of the same i, which the loop keeps changing (and which may go out of scope) before the threads read it
Fix: pass a separate value per thread, e.g. an array element args[i] or the value cast into the pointer

items.expected_concept: a thread must not return a pointer to its own stack; the joiner receives it through pthread_join
items.question: A thread function computes a result in a local struct and returns its address; main reads it after pthread_join. What is wrong, and what should the thread return instead?
answer: The local struct lives on the thread's stack, which is gone once the thread exits, so the pointer dangles
Return heap-allocated memory (or a value) and collect it via the second argument of pthread_join

items.expected_concept: counter++ is a non-atomic load-add-store; interleavings lose updates
items.question: Two threads each execute counter++ one million times on a shared counter starting at 0. The final value is often below 2,000,000. Explain why.
answer: counter++ is several machine instructions (load, add, store), not one atomic step
A context switch between load and store lets both threads store the same value, losing an increment (a race condition)

items.expected_concept: check-then-act on shared data without mutual exclusion is a race; the critical section must be protected
items.question: Two threads run: if (balance >= 100) balance -= 100;  with balance = 100. How can the balance end at -100, and what part of the code is the critical section?
answer: Both threads can pass the check before either subtracts, so both subtract (a race condition)
The check and the update together form the critical section and must execute under mutual exclusion

items.expected_concept: a flag-based lock fails because test and set are separate steps; test-and-set makes them atomic
items.question: A lock is implemented as: while (flag == 1) ; flag = 1;  Why can two threads both enter the critical section, and what hardware instruction fixes this?
answer: A thread can be interrupted between seeing flag == 0 and setting flag = 1, so both see 0 and both enter
An atomic instruction such as test-and-set (or compare-and-swap) reads and sets the flag in one indivisible step

items.expected_concept: spin when the critical section is short and threads run on different cores; otherwise sleep
items.question: On a single-core machine, a thread waits for a lock held by another thread that will hold it for a long time. Which is the better choice?

options.A: Spin, because spinning has no context-switch cost
options.B: Sleep (block), because spinning wastes the only CPU the lock holder needs

items.expected_concept: a semaphore used as a lock is initialised to 1
items.question: To use a semaphore s as a mutual-exclusion lock with sem_wait(&s) before and sem_post(&s) after the critical section, what initial value should s have?

items.expected_concept: a semaphore initialised to 0 makes a thread wait for an event (ordering)
items.question: Thread A must not print "world" until thread B has printed "hello". Using one semaphore, give its initial value and where each thread calls sem_wait / sem_post.
answer: Initial value 0
B calls sem_post after printing hello; A calls sem_wait before printing world, so A blocks until B posts

items.expected_concept: re-check the condition in a while loop because wakeups do not guarantee the condition holds (Mesa semantics, spurious wakeups)
items.question: A consumer does: lock(m); if (count == 0) cond_wait(&c, &m); take(); unlock(m);  With two consumers this sometimes takes from an empty buffer. Why, and what one-word change fixes it?
answer: After being woken, another consumer may already have taken the item, so the condition no longer holds when this one runs (signal is only a hint)
Change if to while so the condition is re-checked after every wakeup

items.expected_concept: cond_wait takes the mutex to release it atomically with going to sleep, preventing a missed wakeup
items.question: Why does pthread_cond_wait take the mutex as an argument, and what goes wrong if a thread checked the condition and then slept without holding the lock?
answer: cond_wait releases the mutex and puts the thread to sleep atomically, and re-acquires it before returning
Without the lock, a signal can arrive between the check and the sleep, so the wakeup is missed and the thread may sleep forever

items.expected_concept: in bounded buffer, waiting on empty/full while holding the mutex deadlocks
items.question: A producer does sem_wait(&mutex); sem_wait(&empty); put(); sem_post(&mutex); sem_post(&full);  When the buffer is full this deadlocks. Explain why and give the correct order.
answer: The producer sleeps on empty while holding mutex; the consumer needs mutex to remove an item, so neither can proceed
Wait on empty first, then mutex: sem_wait(&empty); sem_wait(&mutex); put(); sem_post(&mutex); sem_post(&full)

items.expected_concept: dining philosophers deadlocks by circular wait; break it by changing the acquisition order for one philosopher
items.question: Each of five philosophers picks up the left fork and then the right fork. Why can this deadlock, and give one change that prevents it.
answer: If all pick up their left fork at once, each waits forever for the right fork held by a neighbour (circular wait)
Break the cycle, e.g. one philosopher picks up the right fork first (or allow at most four to sit, or pick up both forks atomically)

items.expected_concept: acquiring locks in one global order removes circular wait
items.question: transfer(a, b) locks a then b. Two threads call transfer(x, y) and transfer(y, x) concurrently and sometimes hang. Which fix removes the deadlock?

options.A: Add sleep() between the two lock calls
options.B: Always lock the two accounts in a fixed global order (e.g. by account id)
options.C: Use a spinlock instead of a mutex

items.expected_concept: an atomicity violation: a check and a use that must be atomic are interrupted; fix with a lock around both
items.question: Thread 1: if (p->info) fputs(p->info, f);  Thread 2: p->info = NULL;  The program sometimes crashes. Name this bug type and the fix.
answer: An atomicity-violation bug: the check and the use were meant to be atomic, but thread 2 can set NULL between them
Protect both the check-and-use and the assignment with the same lock
